items.followUp: A wire of original length 2 m stretches by 4 mm. Calculate its tensile strain.

rubric.why: Checks that strain is defined as a ratio of extension to original length.
rubric.description: Defines tensile strain as extension divided by original length.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio.

rubric.why: Checks the required mathematical expression.
rubric.description: Writes the formula for tensile strain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

modelAnswer: Tensile strain is the ratio of the increase in length of a body to its original length when it is stretched.
Tensile strain = extension/original length = ΔL/L.

items.followUp: A moving ball collides with a stationary ball. Describe what happens to the total momentum of the two balls.

rubric.why: Checks the law's statement that total momentum is conserved.
rubric.description: States that the total momentum of a system remains constant when no external force acts on it.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the conservation statement, including the no-external-force condition.

rubric.why: Checks that the example involves balls before collision.
rubric.description: Identifies the example of a moving ball colliding with a stationary ball.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for setting up the balls example.

rubric.why: Checks that the example demonstrates conservation.
rubric.description: Explains that momentum is transferred between the balls while their combined momentum remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the unchanged total momentum.

modelAnswer: The law of conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of a system remains constant if no external force acts on it.
For example, when a moving ball collides with a stationary ball, the moving ball transfers momentum to the other ball.
The total momentum of the two balls before collision equals their total momentum after collision.
m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

items.followUp: State the second condition for equilibrium and explain what it prevents a body from doing.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of equilibrium as absence of an unbalanced force, with a body at rest or moving uniformly.
rubric.description: Defines equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Checks the first condition in its standard form.
rubric.description: States that the vector sum of all forces acting on the body is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the condition.

rubric.why: Checks the physical meaning of the first condition.
rubric.description: Explains that the body has no linear acceleration and is in translational equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the explanation.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when it has no resultant force acting on it and no resultant turning effect; it remains at rest or moves with uniform velocity.
The first condition for equilibrium is that the vector sum of all forces acting on the body is zero: ΣF = 0.
Thus, the forces balance and the body has no linear acceleration; this is called translational equilibrium.

items.followUp: A 2 kg object is thrown vertically upwards at 10 m s⁻¹. Find its maximum gravitational potential energy and its kinetic energy when it returns to the starting point, neglecting air resistance.

rubric.why: Checks conversion of the given mass to SI units and identification of the initial speed.
rubric.description: Writes the given data in SI units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for m = 0.5 kg and u = 15 m s⁻¹.

rubric.why: Checks the energy relation used to find the potential energy at maximum height.
rubric.description: Uses conservation of mechanical energy: maximum P.E. equals the initial K.E.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relation or equivalent working.

rubric.why: Checks correct substitution and maximum potential energy.
rubric.description: Calculates the maximum P.E.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 56.25 J with correct working.

rubric.why: Checks that the kinetic energy on returning to the ground equals the initial kinetic energy.
rubric.description: Calculates the K.E. when the stone hits the ground.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the correct energy relation, working and answer.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 500 g = 0.5 kg; initial velocity u = 15 m s⁻¹.
At maximum height, the initial K.E. has been converted into P.E., so P.E. = ½mu².
Neglecting air resistance, the K.E. when the stone hits the ground equals its initial K.E.

items.followUp: A force of 60 N acts on an area of 2 cm². Calculate the pressure in pascals.

rubric.why: Checks identification of the force and contact area given in the question.
rubric.description: Writes the given data.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for F = 75 N and A = 1.5 cm².

rubric.why: Checks conversion of area to SI units.
rubric.description: Converts the area from cm² to m².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct conversion.

rubric.why: Checks the formula for pressure.
rubric.description: Writes P = F/A.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: Checks substitution of the force and SI area into the formula.
rubric.description: Substitutes the values with SI units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct substitution.

rubric.why: Checks the calculated pressure and its unit.
rubric.description: Gives the pressure in pascals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 5 × 10⁵ Pa.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 75 N; A = 1.5 cm² = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m².
Formula: P = F/A.
Pressure under the thumb = 5 × 10⁵ Pa.

items.followUp: Define a base unit and give one example of a derived unit.

rubric.why: Checks that a base unit is defined as independent or fundamental.
rubric.description: Defines base units as independent units for fundamental quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition.

rubric.why: Checks that derived units are formed from base units.
rubric.description: Defines derived units as units obtained by combining base units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition; a correct example may support it.

modelAnswer: Base units are independent units used for fundamental physical quantities, such as the metre and kilogram.
Derived units are formed by combining base units, such as m s⁻¹ for velocity.

items.followUp: When the jaws of a vernier callipers are closed, its vernier zero lies to the right of the main-scale zero. Name the zero error and state its sign.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of positive zero error.
rubric.description: Defines positive zero error as occurring when the vernier zero is to the right of the main-scale zero with the jaws closed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Checks the definition of negative zero error.
rubric.description: Defines negative zero error as occurring when the vernier zero is to the left of the main-scale zero with the jaws closed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

modelAnswer: Positive zero error occurs when the jaws are closed and the zero of the vernier scale lies to the right of the zero of the main scale.
Negative zero error occurs when the jaws are closed and the zero of the vernier scale lies to the left of the zero of the main scale.

items.followUp: What does the prefix kilo mean? Give its value as a power of ten and one example of its use.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning and use of prefixes with units.
rubric.description: Defines prefixes as words or symbols placed before units to show multiples or submultiples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Checks that examples correctly pair prefixes with powers of ten.
rubric.description: Gives two correct examples of prefixes and their values.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correct examples.

modelAnswer: Prefixes are words or symbols written before a unit to indicate a multiple or submultiple of that unit.
Examples: kilo = 10³ and milli = 10⁻³.
